[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r1] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The sixth proposed aspect of the Quran's inimitability is its knowledge of the unseen and its truthful forecasts of future events.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | prefers | Al-Mawardi concludes that all eight proposed aspects jointly make the Quran inimitable; none is uniquely preferable, and together they heighten its eloquence and concision.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r11] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | Because of its inimitable form and meanings, Quranic wording needs careful, sustained reflection rather than reliance on first impressions; meanings may become clear or subtle at different times.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r2] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | As evidence of foreknowledge, Jews were challenged to wish for death if the afterlife belonged exclusively to them, then told they would never wish for it because of their deeds; none did so. | mentions 2:94, 2:95
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r3] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The challenge to Quraysh predicted they would not produce a comparable surah, and they did not, another example of a fulfilled forecast.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r4] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | A seventh aspect is that the Quran gathers knowledge beyond the capacities of the Arabs, their speech, or any scholar among other nations, and no other book contains it all.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r5] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | holds | The claims that nothing is omitted from the Book and that it explains everything support the Quran's comprehensive knowledge. | mentions 6:38, 16:89
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r6] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · رسول الله صلى الله عليه وسلم | reports | The Prophet describes the Quran as containing news of the past and reports of what comes after, as truth rather than jest, and says seeking guidance elsewhere leads astray; no grading is stated.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r7] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | An eighth account locates the Quran's inimitability in sarfa: God turned their resolve away from answering the challenge to produce a surah like it.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r8] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · القائلون بهذه الصرفة | reports | One sarfa view says people were stripped of the ability to compose a rival; even if they tried, they would fail.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v1p32/r9] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · القائلون بهذه الصرفة | reports | The other sarfa view says people were diverted from attempting a rival despite having the ability, so they might have succeeded if they tried.
[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p402/r10] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | The question may ask whether he knows the unseen and thus saw that what he heard was false.

[MAWARDI-FULL:v5p402/r12] MAWARDI-FULL, d. 450 · author | reports | A further possibility is that he knew there is no resurrection and therefore expected no recompense.

[RAZI-FULL:v29p11#2/r5] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The question exposes the turner's ignorance and need, and the ugliness of turning away when he ought to heed; unseen knowledge is knowledge of what is hidden from creatures.

[RAZI-FULL:v29p11#2/r7] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | One possible object of يرى is the belief that one person's burden is carried by another: the man supposes this while unaware that each bears only his own. | mentions 53:38
[RAZI-FULL:v29p11#2/r8] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | reports | Alternatively, يرى has no expressed object and means that the man sees his own judgment as sufficient, needing neither guide nor warner.
[RAZI-FULL:v29p11/r4] RAZI-FULL, d. 606 · author | holds | The question about unseen knowledge answers 53:30: the man's limited worldly knowledge is no knowledge of the unseen or of the afterlife. | mentions 53:30

[ABUHAYYAN-FULL:v10p22/r17] ABUHAYYAN-FULL, d. 745 · قيل | reports | Another view says he knows his own condition in the afterlife.
